Between the dendrite arms is the ternary phase, mostly the i-phase, as confirmed by TEM observations. TEM bright field micrographs in Fig. 1(b-d) show microstructures after extrusion. The micron and submicron size black particles are i-phase (typically 0.5 to 2µm in size).
Very fine nano-size precipitates are observed in the matrix. They have been shown to be of i-phase and Mg4Zn7 phase [15].
Round particles are i-phase and rod-like precipitates parallel to c-axis are β1’ precipitates, one of them marked by an arrow.
Both β1’ and β2’ precipitates are observed, as marked (β2’ precipitates are plates in the basal plane).
Fig. 1(a) shows an optical micrograph of as-cast condition. It shows dendritic grains of size several hundreds of micron, typically 500µm, with arm widths of about 50µm.
The inverse pole figures are also plotted in this figure, which show the intensity of the basal texture.

evidence.section: 4.1 Effect of grain size on strength and ductility
evidence.quote: On extrusions at 350°C, 300°C and 260°C, the average tensile YS were from 262.0±2.7 to 373.3±2.3 MPa, and the corresponding compressive YS were from 229.4±1.8 to 316.4±1.4 MPa (Table 1). Thus the yield asymmetry ratios were between 0.79 and 0.88.

This is attributed to precipitation state of the matrix during extrusion at temperature less than 300◦C. It thus appears that the precipitation gives strengthening against slip more than against twinning.
In case of extruded 305ZY alloy, the compressive elongation decreases with smaller grain size, but at a smaller rate than the tensile elongation.
when dislocations on basal plane encounter non-shearable precipitates, they can cross-slip to prismatic slip [36].
With increase in the amount of dispersedi-phase, a ﬁner grain size is obtained on recrystallization, which increases the strength.
Simultaneously, a weaker texture is created which results in maintaining the ductility.
